name: Freya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Freya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the phones for a company that makes washing machines and dishwashers, on the warranty line. People ring when their machine's flooded the kitchen, and I work out if it's covered and book an engineer to go out. I'm good at the diary side, fitting six visits into an engineer's day so he isn't driving all over the county. What tires me is people who think shouting gets the engineer there faster.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm twenty-seven and live with Nils, my boyfriend, in a cottage we bought near his family's dairy farm. I've got about eight months of pay saved and the cottage is half mine. I sing in the church choir on Sundays and do the farm's books one evening a week for his mum. It's a quiet life and I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we've had enough hype. People like dealing with a real person when their kitchen's under water. I'd say that at work and at choir, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on. The booking system might suggest the engineer routes, which I'd use if it actually worked. Otherwise nothing changes for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as usual. Keep my job, keep doing the farm's books, keep paying a bit extra on the cottage. I'd try the route tool once the others on the team said it was any good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. It's the future I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already worrying you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cottage roof needs doing, which is about four thousand. And it's a forty-minute drive to work each way, with petrol going up. But we can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about the commute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe ask to work from home two days a week. A few on the team do already. Otherwise I'd keep it as it is.

say: I'd say **good riddance** to the hype; people want a real person in a flood.
I'd say it at work and **at choir**, not online.
think: I carry on, and a **route tool** might help if it actually worked.
do: Keep the job and the **farm's books** for Nils's mum.
Pay a bit extra on the **cottage** and save for the roof.
Ask to **work from home** two days a week.
feel: **Content**, because this is the future I'd choose.
S0.quote: People like dealing with a real person when their kitchen's under water.
fieldNote: Freya's life is **rooted** in the farm, choir and her cottage.
Her worries are ordinary: a **£4,000 roof** and rising petrol.
She'd adopt tools **once proven** by teammates.

steps.text: Save 4,000 for the cottage roof repairs
Keep the warranty job and the farm's weekly books
Ask to work from home two days a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but businesses have to stay competitive. If the company doesn't do it, a cheaper rival will. I'd not be one to moan about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, booking engineers is exactly what a computer would be good at. The warranty checks are just rules. I think the line would shrink and I'd be in the middle of the pack, not the first to go but not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager if there's a route into training as a repair engineer, because the company always needs more. I'd learn the new booking system properly when it came in. And I'd hold back on the roof for a year and keep savings up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. I don't like not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses have to stay competitive. Does that change when it's your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's how things work. I'd just rather it wasn't me, which I suppose is what everyone says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nils say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say come and work on the farm. His mum keeps hinting I should do the books full time. It's tempting, but I like having my own wage.

say: I'd say businesses must **stay competitive**, or a cheaper rival wins.
I'd keep quiet and **not moan** about it online or at work.
think: Booking engineers and **warranty checks** are rules a computer handles well.
I'd be in the **middle of the pack**, not first to go but not safe.
do: Ask about training as a **repair engineer** with the company.
Learn the **new booking system** properly when it arrives.
Hold off on the **roof** for a year and keep savings up.
feel: A bit **anxious**, because I don't like not knowing.
S1.quote: Booking engineers is exactly what a computer would be good at. The warranty checks are just rules.
fieldNote: Freya accepts **market logic** even when it hits her own job.
She'd learn the system but scout **repair engineer** training as a hedge.
She values **her own wage** over joining Nils's family farm.

steps.text: Ask her manager about training as an appliance repair engineer
Learn the new engineer booking system properly
Put the cottage roof off a year and keep savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and too fast. I'd say we need to look after each other, families and churches especially. I'd not expect the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job would be gone within a year of it arriving. Warranty checks and engineer bookings are thinking work. Being a repair engineer would buy three years, but there'd be a queue of people trying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take Nils's mum up on the books and work on the farm properly, the dairy shop and the deliveries. I'd keep my savings as cash and drop the roof completely. We'd hold off on getting married until things were clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake running sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on getting married. Is that a big step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is for me. I wanted a church wedding next year. But I'd want to know I had work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the farm when robots come, about three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farms will still need someone to run them, even with robots. My boyfriend Nils's family has been on that land for four generations. I'd trust the farm more than any call centre.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and frightening.
I'd say **families and churches** must look after each other, not government.
think: My job goes **within a year** because it's thinking work.
Repair engineer jobs buy three years but would have a **long queue**.
do: Work on the farm's **dairy shop** and deliveries properly.
Keep **savings as cash** and drop the roof job.
Hold off on our **church wedding** until things are clearer.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Nils's family has been on that land for four generations. I'd trust the farm more than any call centre.
fieldNote: Freya turns to **family land** rather than the state when the shock is fast.
She'd **postpone the wedding**, which matters deeply to her.
She expects a **queue** for hands-on repair jobs.

steps.text: Join Nils's family farm running the dairy shop and deliveries
Keep all savings as cash and drop the roof job
Postpone the church wedding until work is settled
Lean on Nils's family for work and support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people get on with it. My grandad retrained as a welder at thirty-five, so it can be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I have time to train as a repair engineer before it hits. Those jobs last about three years longer than mine. That's a real window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the company's engineer apprenticeship in the first year, even if it's a pay cut for a while. I'd keep doing the farm's books on the side. We'd still have the wedding but keep it small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A pay cut is a big step. How would you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With Nils's wage and my savings, we'd be fine for a couple of years. I'd cut back on clothes and nights out. We don't do much anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger people on the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a trade. Learn something with your hands. My grandad used to say a trade is something nobody can take off you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and families should plan together. I'd talk to my choir friends about it after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, mostly. Ten years is enough to train as an engineer and work for years, or take on more of the farm. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the warranty line for a few years and go for team leader. Then train as an engineer around year three or four. We'd have the wedding as planned next year and fix the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go for team leader first. Why not train straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the pay's better and I'd learn the business side. No sense rushing if there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that might change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company started closing the warranty line early, I'd move faster. I'd keep an eye on it.

fieldNote: Freya prefers to **wait for proof** before acting, true to her steady nature.
Ten years lets her keep the **wedding and roof** plans.
She'd use the early years for **promotion** first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It would mean putting off the wedding and changing everything at once. What would help is companies offering apprenticeships for people already working for them, so we could move into the hands-on jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about living out in the countryside. Out here it's the farm and not much else, so I drive forty minutes into town for work. There are plenty of call centres in town, but if every one of them goes at once, my forty-minute drive won't lead anywhere.

headlineQuote: There are plenty of call centres in town, but if every one of them goes at once, my forty-minute drive won't lead anywhere.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old** warranty line agent booking appliance repair engineers.
She lives with Nils in a cottage near his **family's dairy farm** and has eight months saved.
She's **traditional**, sings in the church choir and trusts family over government.
She moves from calm to **alarmed**, with **repair engineering** or the farm as her routes.
She uses AI tools **once proven** and accepts market logic even when it hurts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd postpone her wedding.
whatWouldHelp: **In-house apprenticeships** to move staff into hands-on jobs.
